title: const and constexpr
summary: `const` means "this value never changes after it is set". `constexpr` means "this value is known **while compiling**". Use them wherever you can: they prevent mistakes and cost nothing.
markdown:
## `const`: a locked box Most values in a program never need to change after they are set. Marking them `const` lets the compiler enforce that. ```cpp const double gravity{ 9.81 }; gravity = 10.0; // error: you cannot assign to a const variable ``` ``` ┌──────────────┐ │ 9.81 │ gravity (locked: read only) └──────────────┘ ``` Two rules: - A `const` variable must be given its value when it is created. - That value may come from anywhere, including the keyboard. It simply cannot change afterwards. ```cpp int age{}; std::cin >> age; const int ageNextYear{ age + 1 }; // set once while running, then locked ``` > [!tip] Make things `const` by default > When you read `const` on a variable, you know its value at every later line without checking. In a long function that is a real help. Leave `const` off only when the value has to change. ## `constexpr`: worked out by the compiler Some values are known before the program ever runs: the number of seconds in a day, the size of a chess board. `constexpr` asks the compiler to calculate them during the build. ```cpp constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; constexpr int secondsPerDay{ 24 * 60 * 60 }; // the compiler stores 86400 int x{}; std::cin >> x; constexpr int bad{ x * 2 }; // error: x is not known while compiling ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph CT["While compiling"] A["constexpr int s{ 24 * 60 * 60 }"] --> B["86400 is written
straight into the program"] end subgraph RT["While running"] C["const int a{ input + 1 }"] --> D["worked out during the run,
then locked"] end ``` You will hear these two phases called **compile time** and **run time**. The distinction comes up again and again in C++. | | `const` | `constexpr` | |---|---|---| | Can change after it is set | No | No | | Value may come from input while running | Yes | No | | Calculated during the build | Sometimes | Always | | Use it for | Any value you will not modify | True constants: `pi`, `maxPlayers`, `gridSize` | ## `constexpr` functions A function can be `constexpr` too. That means the compiler **may** run it during the build when its arguments are known. ```cpp #include constexpr int square(int n) { return n * n; } int main() { constexpr int a{ square(5) }; // worked out while compiling: 25 int side{}; std::cin >> side; int b{ square(side) }; // the same function, used while running std::cout << a << ' ' << b << '\n'; return 0; } ``` One function serves both purposes. ## Replace magic numbers with names A **magic number** is a bare number in the code with no explanation. ```cpp total = price * 1.08; // what is 1.08? ``` ```cpp constexpr double salesTaxRate{ 0.08 }; total = price * (1.0 + salesTaxRate); ``` The second version explains itself. And when the rate changes, you change one line instead of hunting for every `1.08`. ## Sharing constants between files Constants that several files need go in a header, grouped under a name: ```cpp // constants.h #pragma once namespace constants { inline constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; inline constexpr int maxPlayers{ 4 }; } ``` Any file that includes the header writes `constants::pi`. Take the `namespace` and `inline` parts on trust for now. Both are explained in Milestone 3: [[3.05 Scope, Lifetime and Namespaces]] and [[3.06 Global Variables, static and Linkage]]. ## `const` parameters A parameter can be `const` as well: the function promises not to change it. ```cpp void printPrice(const double price) ``` For a simple value that is copied anyway, this is optional. It becomes important with references, where it means "I will look at your data but not alter it": [[4.03 References]].
ideas:
1. Create `constexpr` constants for minutes per hour, hours per day and days per week. Compute seconds per week from them as another `constexpr`.
2. Try to modify a `const` variable and read the error.
3. Write `constexpr int cube(int n)` and use it once with a literal and once with a value read from the keyboard.

cards.q: Can a `const` variable get its value from user input?
cards.a: Yes. It is set once while the program runs and cannot change afterwards. A `constexpr` variable cannot, because its value must be known while compiling.
An unexplained number written directly in the code. Replace it with a named constant.

cards.q: What is the difference between compile time and run time?
cards.a: Compile time is while the program is being built. Run time is while it is running.

cards.q: Does a `constexpr` function always run during the build?
cards.a: No. It can, when its arguments are known then. With values only known while running, it runs like any other function.
